# dsh-ai-terminal-pet

**English** · [中文](./README.zh.md)

A DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Cordis bundle that mirrors Harness session state onto
the [AI Terminal Pet](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet) desktop
overlay: a small always-on-top Win32 pet that shows which sessions are working,
which one is waiting for your approval, which failed, and which finished.

The package ships the overlay binary and the official reporter protocol module
inside the tarball, so a single market install is enough to get a pet on screen
that follows **this Harness's** sessions. It does not attach to any other
terminal by itself: sessions from OpenCode, Claude Code and Antigravity appear
only after that terminal's own reporter is installed into it. The repository
README section [Connect your terminal](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet#connect-your-terminal)
has one hook per terminal; the panel, the pipe and the protocol are shared, so
once a terminal reports it shows up next to the Harness sessions.

No npm dependencies, no install scripts, no network calls at runtime (unless the
maintainer pins a release in lib/release-pins.json, see below).

## What it does

| Harness signal | Overlay state |
| --- | --- |
| `turn/start`, `agent/inbox/claimed`, `agent/status` running | working |
| `tool/call` | tool_use |
| `approval/request` (waterfall listener) | waiting_permission |
| `tool/result` with `error`, `agent/error` | error |
| `turn/end`, `agent/status` idle | idle |
| Harness process exit | closed |

Events this table does not list are not part of the Harness session log: there is
no `command/done` or `working-directory/change` in `SessionEventMap`. The project
path, the parent session and the session start time do not come from events at
all - they are read from `session.header` (`cwd`, `parentSession`, `createdAt`),
which is the only place the host states them. That is also why a session shows
the right project even though the desktop Harness itself runs from its install
directory, and why a subagent conversation is nested under the session it was
forked from.

The overlay then plays an alert tone, shows a tray balloon on those transitions
and its one-click jump button targets the Harness window. Plugin reload (HMR)
disposes the listeners but deliberately does not close sessions: only a real
process exit means the conversation is over.

Panel gestures (overlay 1.0.5 and later): clicking a session row - or the left
half of the compact strip - copies that conversation's working directory to the
clipboard and shows a short "Copied" receipt over the row; clicking anywhere
else still collapses the panel. The copy is the path, not the label the row
prints.

![Copy receipt](../../docs/assets/overlay-copy.png)
*The receipt after a click on a session row: the path is on the clipboard and the
row says so for about a second. A failed copy says "Copy failed" instead of
claiming success.*

## Where it is listed, and what each market indexes

Three independent paths exist today, and each one reads a different field:

| Market | What it indexes | What this package offers it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| npm registry | package name, version, `dist.integrity` | published as `dsh-ai-terminal-pet`; a market that installs by name gets a verified tarball |
| dshmarket (the market tab most Harness Desktop users run) | `https://awesome-dsh-plugin.com/plugins.json`, which is generated from the [awesome-dsh-plugin](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin) repository | entry merged via PR [#13937](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/13937); the `install` command it renders comes from that entry's pinned `tarball`, so bumping it is always a pull request *there*, never an edit here |
| GitHub-harvesting markets | repositories carrying the `dsh-plugin` topic plus a root `package.json` declaring `name` and `dsh.bundle` | this repository has the topic and the root shim manifest, which is what makes `dsh plugin add github:owner/repo` resolve instead of mounting a 0.0.0 dependency |

"Listed" and "visible" are different states, and only the second one helps a
user: the awesome entry existed before its `plugins.json` entry did, because the
site builds the catalog on a schedule. Check the market's own public index, not
the merged pull request. The package README cannot promise what another
repository's build will render; it can only promise that the fields those builds
read are present and correct.

The package describes itself to storefronts through `dsh.catalog`: a category, a
one-line summary in both languages, and the capabilities it uses. Capabilities
are self-declared and never checked — DSH does not sandbox plugins — so read them
as a description, not a permission grant.
The bundle is Windows only and declares `dsh.bundle.platforms: ["win32"]`, so
other platforms show it as unsupported instead of installing it.

It also declares `dsh.marketplace` (`profiles: ["desktop", "headless", "web"]`,
`requiresBuildApproval: false`, `manualSteps: false`). DSH itself never reads
that field - the bundle mounts through `dsh.bundle` either way - but storefronts
that sort entries by profile do: without it a registry falls back to a
headless-or-web guess and a desktop client hides the entry.

Manually, from a terminal, into a profile you own — by package name, by release
tarball, or by pinning the release tag. All three are verified end to end:

```sh
# by package name: published on npm, no clone, no Go toolchain
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-ai-terminal-pet

# release tarball: same bytes as the npm release, straight from the GitHub Release
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/download/dsh-plugin-v1.2.17/dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.17.tgz

# git source, pinned to the release tag
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add "git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git#dsh-plugin-v1.2.17&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet"
```

Those three differ only in transport. The npm path is the shortest and the one a
market uses when it installs by name; the tarball path works when a market pins a
release asset instead of a registry entry; the git path is the fallback for a
machine that cannot reach npm at all. Every one of them lands the same
prebuilt overlay in `vendor/`.

Do not hand pnpm a bare repository URL. pnpm resolves a git dependency by
running the package's lifecycle scripts, and it blocks those for unpinned
git sources until you copy the `allowBuilds` key it prints into your profile's
`pnpm-workspace.yaml`; the failure message never mentions AI Terminal Pet. The
package therefore ships no lifecycle hook, and its vendored overlay is a
committed file rather than a build product. `vendor/manifest.json` records the
SHA-256 of that file, the SHA-256 of the Go sources it was built from, and the
Go version that produced it, so a stale or hand-edited vendor directory fails a
check instead of shipping quietly.

The GitHub and npm paths above need nothing from this repository at install time.
`dsh plugin add dsh-ai-terminal-pet` resolves through the npm registry; the
tarball and git forms resolve through GitHub. A marketplace that indexes npm
sees the package under its own name and can verify the published integrity
digest; a marketplace that indexes repositories sees the `dsh-plugin` topic and
the root shim manifest.

`add` is the whole install: the profile records the dependency, and the bundle
declares itself through `dsh.bundle.patch`, so no separate `enable` step exists.
The profile you add it to has to be the one Harness boots.

Two profiles are special. The reserved `desktop` profile is rejected by the
standalone `dsh` CLI (`profile "desktop" is managed exclusively by the Electron
application`); the Desktop app's own bundled CLI does accept it, and the in-app
plugin manager is the supported path there. Any other profile name is yours.

If the app reports restart-required after enabling the bundle, restart Harness.

## What it writes on disk

First use in a Harness process copies two files, and only when they are missing:

| File | Origin | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| %LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js | vendor/protocol.js | pipe name, state set, redaction, snapshot |
| %LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe | vendor/AI-Terminal-Pet.exe | the Win32 overlay |

Nothing is ever overwritten: an existing file, including one placed by the
standalone installer, wins. Set DSH_PET_NO_BOOTSTRAP=1 to skip this step
entirely (for example when the overlay is managed by `scripts/install.ps1` already).

Reports also write the overlay's normal runtime snapshot under the same
directory, exactly like every other reporter.

### Optional download fallback

lib/release-pins.json is absent from the published package by default. When the
maintainer fills it in with pinned release asset URLs, sizes and SHA-256
digests, a machine that has no vendored binary downloads the two assets over
HTTPS with a 30 s timeout, verifies size and digest with node:crypto, and only
then installs them. Any failure is silent apart from one warning; the plugin
keeps working without an overlay.

## The overlay itself is still standalone

This bundle is a convenience. The overlay is a Go application that installs
normally with `scripts/install.ps1` from the repository, and every other reporter
(Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity, generic) talks to the same named pipe.
Those reporters are separate installs, not part of this package: a terminal that
has none of them hooked reports nothing, in this install or in any other. A
machine that only wants the overlay does not need this package; a machine that
only wants the plugin gets one installed automatically.

## Requirements and limits

- Windows only (named pipes plus a Win32 layered window).
- DeepSeek Harness 0.2.x. `engines.dsh` is `>=0.2.0-0 <0.3.0-0`, and since DSH
  0.2.1-alpha.3 the host reads that range alone: a bundle whose range the running
  DSH does not satisfy is refused and the profile rolled back, so the range is the
  whole compatibility statement. The `-0` bounds are deliberate - DSH evaluates
  the range with semver's `includePrerelease`, under which `<0.3.0` still admits
  `0.3.0-rc.1` and `>=0.2.0` still refuses `0.2.0-rc.1`. Both ends were measured
  against the host's own compatibility function. It was verified by installing
  this tarball into a real 0.2.0-rc.1 host and a real 0.2.2-rc.3 host and
  composing its layer with `dsh --dump-config`.
- Node 24.9+ in the Harness runtime, which is what DSH 0.2.x itself requires.
- Nothing in this package can fail the host: every entry point is wrapped,
  every report is fire-and-forget, and there is no process.exit.
- Session id is the Harness session.header.id; pid is a synthetic per-session
  id and parentPid is the real Harness process, which is how the overlay ties a
  session to its terminal window.

# ai-terminal-pet

Stop glancing across terminal windows to track agent states. It costs one small executable with no account and no cloud.

![ai-terminal-pet](docs/assets/hero.png)

![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows-blue) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/go-1.23-00ADD8) ![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-1.0.8-blue)
![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green) ![Size](https://img.shields.io/badge/size-4.17%20MiB-blue) ![Dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-3-informational) ![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-206-brightgreen) ![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-ai-terminal-pet?label=dsh%20plugin)

> 🇬🇧 [English](#english)  ·  🇨🇳 [中文](#中文)

---

## English

### The problem

You run Claude Code, OpenCode, or Antigravity in multiple terminal windows at once. A background task prompts for permission to execute a tool, but you are focused in another window and never notice the prompt.

Fourteen minutes later, you switch back only to discover that your build has been sitting idle the entire time. Glancing across multiple terminal tabs wastes focus and breaks your concentration.

ai-terminal-pet anchors a 56px strip to the screen edge. It aggregates your sessions in real time, pulses when an agent needs permission, and displays which project is waiting and for how long.

The table below contrasts the everyday workflow before and after using the overlay:

| Context | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple terminals | Four terminal windows open; you lose track of which window needs attention. | One 56px strip on the edge of the screen aggregates every active session. |
| Blocked build | You find out a build was blocked on a permission prompt fourteen minutes ago. | The overlay pulses immediately and shows which project is waiting and for how long. |
| Context switching | You click across tabs to check whether builds and tasks are still running. | A single glance reveals current states without touching your keyboard or mouse. |

### What it looks like

![Demo](docs/assets/demo.gif)
*The actual sequence: a session blocks on a permission prompt and the strip breathes, hovering unfolds the session list, and clicking the arrow at the end of the waiting row brings that terminal forward. Frames are rasterized from the shipped renderer; the ring stands in for the click, since a layered window draws no cursor.*

![Compact strip](docs/assets/overlay-compact.png)
*Compact strip: pulsing state orb with status glyph, session count, state word, and waiting project name.*

![Expanded list](docs/assets/overlay-expanded.png)
*Expanded list: active sessions showing per-row project name, state, source hook, and relative time.*

![Many sessions](docs/assets/overlay-expanded-many.png)
*Expanded list with many sessions: six session rows followed by the overflow line showing remaining sessions.*

![Auto-approve countdown](docs/assets/overlay-auto-approve.png)
*Auto-approve countdown: draining bar with "Allow (5s)" prompt allowing manual veto before automatic permission approval.*

![In context](docs/assets/desktop-scene.png)
*In context: the strip sits at the screen edge beside two terminals, so a blocked session is visible without switching windows. The panel is the real renderer output; the two terminals around it are drawn, since a real capture would contain somebody's project names.*

---

### Features

The table below outlines the core capabilities and exact runtime parameters of the application:

| Feature | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| State aggregation | Aggregates sessions across 7 states (`idle`, `thinking`, `working`, `tool_use`, `waiting_permission`, `error`, `closed`), showing the highest-priority state across all active sessions. |
| Compact and expanded panels | Compact panel occupies 56x156 logical pixels anchored to a screen edge; clicking expands to 200 px wide, displaying 1–6 rows before adding an overflow line. |
| Copy a project path | Click a session row (or the copy half of the compact strip) to put that conversation's working directory on the clipboard; a short pill over the row confirms it, and a failed copy says so instead of claiming success. Rows whose reporter sent no working directory keep their old meaning: clicking them collapses the panel. |
| Whole-panel gestures | Clicking anywhere that is not a session row or a control toggles compact and expanded; drag anywhere moves 1:1 with the cursor; the wheel zooms between 65% and 160%. |
| Edge retract | Slides mostly off-screen when docked at an edge leaving a thin sliver; hovering restores it, while waiting_permission or error states override retraction to remain visible. |
| Tray menu | Right-click tray menu toggles visibility, resets position and zoom, opens settings, switches language, toggles autostart, and configures auto-approve. |
| Settings window | Native four-tab window (General, Sound, Sessions, Look) where every change persists immediately to `config.json` without an OK button. |
| Synthesized alert tones | Generates 44.1 kHz 16-bit mono PCM WAV tones in memory across four sound schemes (`chime`, `bell`, `soft`, `pulse`), with separate gates for waiting, error, and finish. |
| Per-session alerts | Fires Windows tray notification balloons and audio alerts when a session starts waiting for you, fails, or finishes — one pure policy decides (see below), so a prompt you are already reading does not also pop a balloon. |
| Attentiveness | An alert depends on what the session is asking for and whether you are looking: approval / question / plan review are told apart from the reason reporters already send, keyboard-and-mouse idle time is read from the OS, and the window that owns the session is resolved with the same ranking jump-to-terminal uses. Unmeasurable facts alert rather than stay quiet. |
| Per-session mute and unread | Right-click a session row to mute or unmute that conversation; a suppressed alert still marks its row unread, cleared by jumping to it, by it running again, or by it disappearing. Muting never silences the auto-approve countdown, which is a safety control, not a notification. |
| Alert receipt | The last alert decision is written to `alerts.json` beside `config.json` - not in `runtime/`, where every `*.json` is a reporter snapshot and the scanner deletes what it cannot parse - and printed by `--json` under `alerts` and summarised by the tenth `--doctor` check, so "why was I not told" has an answer instead of folklore. |
| Auto-approve and denylist | Provides a 5-second veto window on permission prompts where a tap denies and silence approves; blocks commands matching the dangerous-command denylist. |
| Jump to terminal | Walks session process ancestry and matches window titles to bring the waiting terminal window or tab to the foreground. |
| Scriptable CLI | Outputs structured session state via `ai-terminal-pet --json` by reading disk snapshots, avoiding blocking on GUI processes. |
| Single instance | A named mutex makes a second launch activate the running overlay instead of starting another one. |
| Connection capacity | The pipe server accepts 32 concurrent connections with a 5 s read timeout, so IPC never blocks the UI thread. |
| Idle lifecycle | A session is dropped only after a 2-minute absence grace; with no session left, the process removes itself after 10 minutes. |

### How it works

```text
Host CLI (Claude Code / OpenCode / Antigravity)
       │
       ▼ (Fire-and-forget hooks)
reporters/*.js
       │
       ▼ (JSON line over Windows named pipe: \\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>)
AI-Terminal-Pet.exe (Go 1.23, single-instance mutex)
       │
       ├─► internal/pipeserver (32 connections, 5s timeout, OK/ERR response)
       ├─► internal/store (in-memory state, TTL, disk snapshots fallback)
       └─► internal/ui (Win32 layered window, GDI topmost canvas)
```

- **Per-user named pipe**: IPC flows through `\\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>`, where `<8hex>` is derived from the SHA-256 hash of the user home directory. The exact same pipe-name algorithm is implemented in Go and JavaScript, locked by a cross-language golden test.

- **JSON line protocol**: Sessions transmit one JSON line per message with a 1 MiB payload cap. The server replies with an exact `OK` or `ERR` acknowledgment, and reporters retry until a deadline without treating partial reads as success.

- **On-disk snapshots**: Snapshot files under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\runtime\` provide a fallback channel and serve as the authoritative on-disk record of active sessions.

- **OS observation over heartbeats**: Session existence is decided by operating system observation of the process table and window titles rather than reporter heartbeats. A session remains active as long as its terminal window exists, and removal requires the host to be unobservable for a continuous 2-minute grace period.

- **Disks beat heartbeats**: The disk snapshot is authoritative for session existence: a session that was on disk and is gone is over, while synthetic PIDs from hooks never participate in liveness probing.

- **Connection handling**: The server accommodates 32 concurrent connections with a 5s read timeout, keeping IPC processing off the UI thread.

- **GDI rendering**: A top-down 32bpp DIB section created with CreateDIBSection is painted through a memory DC and handed to the layered window with UpdateLayeredWindow.

### Install

There are three ways in. Pick the one that matches how you got here.

**A. DeepSeek Harness user — no Go toolchain, nothing to build**

```powershell
dsh plugin add dsh-ai-terminal-pet
```

The package carries a prebuilt overlay and this project's own `protocol.js`. On first load it copies them into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\` **only when they are missing**, so it never overwrites an install you maintain yourself. That is the whole setup: the panel appears on the next session. It is also on npm as [`dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-ai-terminal-pet) (1.2.17), and the release tarball, a tag-pinned git source and a bare repository URL all work (`dsh plugin add <path-or-git-url>`); the same bootstrap runs either way. It targets DeepSeek Harness 0.2.x (`engines.dsh` `>=0.2.0-0 <0.3.0-0`, Node 24.9+); a 0.1.x host is not covered, and such a host refuses the bundle instead of loading it untested.

**B. Everyone else — download a package, no Go toolchain**

Two packages are published for this release: a self-extracting `pet-setup.exe` and a portable zip. Both install the same 11 artifacts into the same directory; the zip additionally lets you look inside before running anything.

1. Download one of them from the [`pet-v1.0.7` release](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/tag/pet-v1.0.8):
   - **`pet-setup.exe`** (14,308,864 B, 13.65 MiB): double-click it. It verifies its own payload against `SHA256SUMS.txt` **before** writing anything, then runs the installer inside itself. `pet-setup.exe --verify` re-checks the installed files at any time, `--uninstall` removes them, `--add-to-path` puts the commands on your PATH.
   - **`ai-terminal-pet-1.0.8-win-x64.zip`** (5,054,322 B, 17 files): unzip it anywhere and double-click `install.cmd`. Everything is inspectable first; `install.cmd -VerifyOnly`, `-Uninstall` and `-AddToPath` work as they do in the source tree.
2. Verify that the installation works:
   ```powershell
   & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
   ```

The zip and the setup exe carry the three binaries, `protocol.js`, the Harness bundle, the installer and a `SHA256SUMS.txt`, so the only thing on Windows is one download and one double-click. Neither needs Go, Node, or an installer framework. The release is **not code-signed yet**, so the first run shows SmartScreen's "unknown publisher" prompt:

![SmartScreen on an unsigned build](docs/assets/smartscreen-unsigned.png)
*What an unsigned build produces on a machine that has never seen it: click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. This image is a reconstruction of the documented dialog, not a capture - see [docs/assets/README.md](docs/assets/README.md).*

That prompt is a certificate the project does not have, not a problem with the file you downloaded — the per-file SHA256 values in `SHA256SUMS.txt` are the honest substitute until a certificate exists.

After installing, `--doctor` should look like this (paths shortened here, everything else is the program's own output):

![--doctor on a healthy install](docs/assets/doctor-green.png)
*Ten checks, and the one that matters when you see an empty panel is `instance` — if it says a live instance is listening, the overlay is healthy and the missing piece is the terminal's reporter, not the install.*

**C. Developers — build from source (Go 1.23+)**

```powershell
# 1. Build the overlay, the native statusline shim and the native hook
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe ./cmd/ai-terminal-pet
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-statusline.exe ./cmd/pet-statusline
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-hook.exe ./cmd/pet-hook

# 2. Install (stops a running overlay, copies, re-hashes every artifact)
.\scripts\install.cmd

# 3. See it work
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
```

Re-verify the installed artifacts at any time with per-file SHA256 checks:

```powershell
.\scripts\install.cmd -VerifyOnly
```

It prints `install: verified - 11 file(s) match the repository, 0 warning(s)` and exits 0 only when every deployed artifact matches (the 11 artifacts are the overlay, the statusline shim, the native hook `pet-hook.exe`, `protocol.js`, and the 7 files of the DeepSeek Harness bundle). The installer itself stops a running overlay first and waits for the process to release its file handles; a plain file copy over a live binary fails at random, which is what the retry loop and the SHA256 comparison after every copy are for.

`install.cmd` is the entry point rather than `install.ps1` because a stock Windows install runs PowerShell at `RemoteSigned`, and `RemoteSigned` refuses a local `.ps1` that still carries the "downloaded from the internet" zone marker — the exact shape of a file you unzip from a release. The wrapper starts one `powershell.exe` with `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`, changes no machine or user policy, forwards every argument and every exit code, and adds no install logic: `install.ps1` remains the only implementation, and `.\scripts\install.ps1 -VerifyOnly` works unchanged on a machine whose policy already allows it.

Put `ai-terminal-pet` on your PATH so you can type the bare command:

```powershell
.\scripts\install.cmd -AddToPath
```

It writes **only** `HKCU\Environment\Path` (never `HKLM`), backs the previous value up to `<install dir>\path-backup.txt` first, and does nothing if the directory is already listed. **Open a new terminal** for the change to take effect. `-Uninstall` also removes that PATH entry, so uninstalling does not leave a dead entry behind (the previous value is backed up again, this time into `%TEMP%`).
Without this step the installer does not touch your PATH at all, so keep using the full path `& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json`.

The installer lives under `scripts/` rather than at the repository root on purpose: market indexers fetch a root `install.ps1` by name and regex-scan it, and this script legitimately mentions the `HKCU` Run key and a `-Recurse -Force` cleanup. Moving it one level down takes those two false positives off the root without taking any behaviour off the script.

Run `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` at any point after installing to self-check the environment, install files, runtime state, pipe, autostart entry, and node availability. To remove the deployed artifacts, run `.\scripts\install.cmd -Uninstall`; it asks for a typed `yes` confirmation first, refuses unsafe target directories, and accepts `-Force` for unattended removal.

Installing a terminal hook is required for that terminal to report; see the next section to connect your tools.

### Connect your terminal

| Terminal | How to connect | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| OpenCode | Add `file:///C:/path/to/ai-terminal-pet/reporters/opencode.js` to `plugins` in `opencode.json` (OpenCode 2.x: the file is a plugin with an `id` and a `setup`) | Turn, tool and permission states, including the difference between "waiting for you" and "still working" |
| Claude Code | Add `& "%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\pet-hook.exe" --mode=claude` for `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, and `Notification` in `settings.json`. `node <repo>/reporters/claude-hook.js` still works and is the fallback when you cannot run the `.exe`. | Real-time status updates, tool execution tracking, and permission prompt alerts |
| Antigravity | Set `statusLine.command` to `pet-statusline.exe` and configure `pet-hook.exe --mode=antigravity` for agent and tool events (`antigravity-hook.js` is the fallback) | Fast statusline updates, agent state changes, and permission request forwarding |
| DeepSeek Harness | Install the Cordis bundle from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\bundles\ai-terminal-pet-bridge\` via the plugin manager (`install_bundle`) | turn/start to working, tool/call to tool_use, approval/asked to waiting_permission, tool/result with an error to error, turn/end to idle, process exit to closed |
| Anything else | Run `node reporters/generic.js` with `--source`, `--state`, and `--project` flags | Instant status reporting from any custom script or CLI tool |

Writing your own reporter for a tool that is not listed here needs no source reading: [docs/PROTOCOL.md](docs/PROTOCOL.md) specifies the wire protocol (fields, state semantics, pipe-name derivation, acknowledgment contract, and redaction rules) that a conforming reporter must implement.

The Harness side is a host-only Cordis bundle: it holds no pipe-name, state-set or snapshot logic of its own, it loads the protocol from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js` and delegates everything to it.

The Harness side has a second, self-contained option since `dsh-ai-terminal-pet` `1.1.0`: a standalone DSH plugin package at [`packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet), also shipped as a GitHub Release asset. # dsh-remedy (plugin)

**Stop losing a whole turn to one fused tool call.** The model occasionally glues
two tool calls into one JSON blob, the adapter cannot parse it, and the turn dies.
This plugin splits the blob at the stream seam into two calls that can run; what
it cannot prove — a truncated tail, a single object, a fragment that does not fit
the tool — keeps its original error instead of being dressed up as a repair. It
also names the deterministic refusals it will not retry, and says nothing when
there is nothing to repair.

Installing this package also installs `dsh-remedy-core`: the plugin pins the
exact version of that engine, so one install resolves both. The split is
deliberate rather than packaging noise — the engine does no I/O and takes no
host, so it can be embedded and tested on its own, while this package owns the
seam, the configuration and the command line. Because the pin is exact, the two
versions always ship together; a version skew is refused before anything is
published.

host, so it can be embedded and tested on its own, while this package owns the
seam, the configuration and the command line. Because the pin is exact, the two
versions always ship together; a version skew is refused before anything is
published.

## Mount

`cordis.patch.yml` adds one row through `insert:`:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: remedy-stream
      name: dsh-remedy
      config:
        repair: true
        retryOnMalformed: 0
        maxCalls: 8
```

`dsh-remedy` must be the **bare** package specifier: the loader resolves
`dist/index.js` from it.

## Config

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `repair` | `true` | Wrap `llm/stream` |
| `retryOnMalformed` | `0` | Retries per step after `MALFORMED_RESPONSE`; a stop-gap, not the fix |
| `maxCalls` | `8` | Ceiling on calls synthesized from one fused block |
| `journalPath` | unset | Append redacted repair events as JSONL; no writes when unset |
| `log` | `true` | One mount line through `ctx.logger` |

## CLI

```
dsh-remedy status  [--json] [--journal <file>]
dsh-remedy repair  [<file>] [--name <tool>] [--id <call-id>] [--max-calls <n>] [--truncated] [--json]
dsh-remedy scan    <session.jsonl|directory> [--since <iso>] [--max-files <n>] [--json] [--out <file>]
dsh-remedy explain [--sessions <dir>] [--profile-file <cordis.patch.yml>]
dsh-remedy verify  [--json]
```

`scan` takes one plain `.jsonl` file, a multi-frame `session.v4.jsonl.zstd` log,
or a directory of them; `--since` drops older events and reports how many it
dropped, `--max-files` caps the walk. It also prints the turn census and the
error codes it counted. `repair` reads stdin when no file is given, and a `.json`
fixture through its `arguments` field. `explain` prints, per failure class this
machine actually hit, how often, which patch covers it, and whether that patch is
switched on in the profile named by `--profile-file`. Three answers are possible
in that last column: the coverers, `(no)` for a profile that switches them off,
and `unknown` when no profile was named — an unread profile is not a finding, so
`explain` exits `0` in that case and `1` only when a profile it read switches
every coverer of a class the host hits off.

Exit codes: `0` ok · `1` finding · `2` usage · `3` unavailable.

`scan --out` writes the report and a `.sha256` sidecar. A report that finds
fusion exits `1`, because a dead turn is a finding even when the file is valid.

## What the wrapper emits

On a proven fusion it replaces the terminal error with:

```
block-end(index=0, id=<original>)
block-end(index=<next>, id=<original>#remedy-1)
...
finish{kind:'stop'}
```

When a fused text glues two calls of different tools, the stream carries one
tool name for that index. A fragment whose arguments do not satisfy the named
tool's declared `required` fields is sent out under **`remedy_unattributed`**;
the runtime answers `UNKNOWN_TOOL` and the turn continues, so the wrong tool is
never called. The repair event records how many fragments that happened to.

Everything else passes through unchanged.

# dsh-remedy

[![CI](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/dsh-remedy/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/dsh-remedy/actions)
[![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-remedy.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-remedy)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
[![Node](https://img.shields.io/badge/node-%3E%3D22.19-brightgreen.svg)](https://nodejs.org)
[![Status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-verified-blue.svg)](#status)

[中文说明](README.zh-CN.md)

dsh-remedy is a patch set for DeepSeek Harness (DSH) — thirty-five defects, each registered with the seam it touches, the symptom it removes, the mechanism that was measured, and the limits it does not cross. Two of those seams are resident (`llm/stream` and `agent/request-error`); the rest are the CLI, the build side, and one seam that has been measured but deliberately not mounted.

## What it fixes

When an upstream provider relay packs two tool calls into one index, `@earendil-works/pi-ai` receives `{...}{...}` and throws. `dsh-llm-pi-ai` converts this into `LlmError(..., 'MALFORMED_RESPONSE')`, and `dsh-agent-loop` aborts the turn because `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` is not in `retryableCodes`. Upstream discussion deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness #4427 describes the same failure family.

```text
Tool call "<name>": Unexpected non-whitespace character after JSON at position N
Received arguments: {...}{...}
```

Measured over this machine's session directory: 78 session files, 393 attempts, 38 fused calls, 44 `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` failures of which 39 are repairable, and 0 unreadable lines.

The turn census of the same directory counted 293 turns: 94 completed, 88 `max_tokens`, 100 error and 11 aborted. The error codes it named are `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` 44, `UNSUPPORTED_REASONING_EFFORT` 37, `SERVER` 16, `UNKNOWN` 1, `MISSING_CREDENTIAL` 1 and `INVALID_REQUEST` 1.

Two of those classes needed different treatment, and both are now visible:

- `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` is a fusion, so it is repaired when the split can be proven.
- `UNSUPPORTED_REASONING_EFFORT` is a deterministic refusal: a profile asked for a level the adapter does not offer (`provider "opendesign" model "deepseek-v4.1-flash-eco" does not support reasoning effort "xhigh"`). Retrying it spends a request to learn the same answer twice, so the plugin names it once and refuses to touch it.

## The patch set, by seam

The registry is the single source: `packages/core/src/registry.ts` for the claims, `dsh-remedy status` to print it, and `dsh-remedy explain` to answer which of them cover a failure class your machine actually hits.

| seam | patches | what each one settles |
|---|---|---|
| `llm/stream` (resident) | P-0001, P-0002, P-0003, P-0005, P-0027, P-0030, P-0033, P-0034 | split a proven fusion; a rescue must be provable, attributable and atomic; a refusal must be observable; reseal a bare member value or refuse it; a fragment dispatched under a name nobody proved; the proof reads the schema the host sends; a call with no identity never reaches the log with an empty id; a stream that failed is never booked as a quiet one |
| `agent/request-error` (resident) | P-0011, P-0013 | the contract for who owns the decision, with a bounded retry budget; name the deterministic refusals instead of retrying them |
| CLI | P-0004, P-0006, P-0009, P-0010, P-0016, P-0025 | scan fidelity and redaction shapes; the turn census; a session header is dated by `createdAt`; the usage text must match the binary; coverage is declared by the patch, not restated by the command; an unread profile is not a finding |
| build side | P-0007, P-0008, P-0012, P-0014, P-0017, P-0018, P-0019, P-0020, P-0021, P-0022, P-0023, P-0024, P-0026, P-0028, P-0029, P-0031, P-0032, P-0035 | a copy channel that can name its failures; a byte budget a script checks; one cap per load path; the project's own description must be true; the two npm pages; a Windows exit code is not a registry answer; the outward pages described a project that had stopped existing; a listing that pins git bytes while advertising a registry version; an export that named a module that never existed; a drift test that repaired the drift; a doc rule no gate read; the two package pages finally inside the copy channel; the release procedure had two homes; the published sample that carried this machine's home path; the live pointers a successor acts on; the engine finally has a budget; the ledger stops repeating its patch docs; a patch-layer row that named a module nothing resolved |
| measured, not mounted | P-0015 | what a rejected `agent/pre-step` decision does, so a later patch can use that seam on measured ground |

Four patches are `verified`: a real host ran them and left a `data/results/live-*` artifact. The other thirty-one are `tested`: unit tests, a negative control and a measured fixture, scan or corpus, but nothing a resident journal can witness. The status section below names which is which.

## Install

Install the plugin into a DSH profile:

```bash
dsh plugin --profile <name> add dsh-remedy
```

Install as a project dependency:

```bash
pnpm add dsh-remedy dsh-remedy-core
```

Version 0.3.0 of the plugin cannot be installed from the registry, because npm published its raw workspace manifest with a literal `workspace:*` dependency. Every release after it ships a pnpm-packed tarball instead. Version 0.3.1 carried the same manifest fix but was superseded before it reached the registry.

Source workflow for contributors:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/dsh-remedy.git
cd dsh-remedy
pnpm install
pnpm run verify
```

## How it works

dsh-remedy buffers incoming tool-call deltas on the `llm/stream` Cordis seam:

```text
Input chunks:
  block-start { id: "call_01", name: "ops_bash" }
  tool-call-delta '{"command":"ls"}{"command":"pwd"}'
  finish { kind: 'error', error: LlmError('MALFORMED_RESPONSE') }

Repaired output:
  block-start { id: "call_01", name: "ops_bash" }
  block-end   { arguments: '{"command":"ls"}' }
  block-start { id: "call_01#remedy-1", name: "ops_bash" }
  block-end   { arguments: '{"command":"pwd"}' }
  finish      { kind: 'stop' }
```

The repair is all-or-nothing. Every open buffer must parse into top-level JSON objects. If all of them are proven, each call gets its own `block-start` and `block-end` and the error finish becomes `{kind:'stop'}`. If any buffer cannot be proven, nothing is emitted and the original failure goes out untouched.

A second listener runs on `agent/request-error`, which the loop calls after a failed attempt:

```text
no code, empty code, or an aborted signal  → next()
UNSUPPORTED_REASONING_EFFORT,              → name it once per step and code, then next()
INVALID_REQUEST, MISSING_CREDENTIAL,
EMPTY_RESPONSE
IMAGE_OFFLOAD_REQUIRED, INVALID_CREDENTIAL → next()
MALFORMED_RESPONSE with budget left        → { kind: 'retry' }
anything else, or budget spent              → next()
```

That order follows the contract the runtime documents: a handling listener returns `{ kind: 'retry' }` **without** calling `next()`, and a listener that does not own the decision must return `next()`. Calling `next()` first and then overriding its answer would discard what the default chain decided, and context compaction authorizes its own retry on exactly that path.

Retry is off by default (`retryOnMalformed: 0`). The budget is a bounded cache of 256 entries per process, which is far more than one turn needs and small enough that a long-lived desktop session cannot grow it.

## Ask it what is happening

`dsh-remedy explain` reads the registry, an optional profile layer and an optional session directory, and prints one row per failure class: how often this machine hit it, which patch covers it, and whether that patch is switched on in the profile you named.

```bash
dsh-remedy explain --sessions ~/.dsh/sessions --profile-file ~/.dsh/profiles/<name>/cordis.patch.yml
```

```text
failure class                turns  covered by          enabled here
---------------------------  -----  -------------------  -------------------
completed                      124  (none)               (none)
max-tokens                      88  by design            no (by design)
MALFORMED_RESPONSE              47  P-0001…P-0005,P-0011 P-0001…P-0005
UNSUPPORTED_REASONING_EFFORT    37  P-0013               P-0013
SERVER                          16  by design            no (by design)
MISSING_CREDENTIAL               1  P-0013               P-0013
```

Without `--sessions` it prints no counts rather than a row of zeros, and without `--profile-file` it says the answer is unknown rather than assuming the default. A class this machine hits, that a patch covers, but that your profile switched off, makes it exit 1.

## Safety guarantees

- Top-level JSON objects are split strictly at depth zero; `}{` inside a JSON string is not a boundary.
- The first split call keeps its original id; synthetic calls receive `<id>#remedy-N`.
- If any buffer cannot be proven, nothing is emitted and the original failure is re-thrown.
- A single object that fails to parse is rejected, never split.
- The plugin mounts only its own rows, adding no route, no tool and no UI.
- The plugin writes nothing to disk unless `journalPath` is configured.
- `retryOnMalformed` defaults to 0 because retry is a stop-gap, not the fix.
- An empty tool name is rejected (`missing-name`) and never dispatched.
- A tool name that changes inside one index aborts the rescue (`name-changed`) and the original failure is re-thrown.
- Adapter `replayState` is preserved across a repaired finish.
- A `block-end` repair is held until the tool-call phase ends; a later rejection in the same stream withdraws it (`rolled-back`) and the original chunks go out.
- `maxCalls` bounds the calls synthesized for the whole stream, not per block.
- A consumer that stops early is recorded as `consumer-abort`, never as quiet.
- A synthesized call is emitted as a `block-start` plus a `block-end`, never a bare `block-end`.
- A withdrawn repair returns its calls to the stream `maxCalls` budget.
- A `max-tokens` stream is counted as truncated, never as an unrepaired fusion.
- A provider error that passes through is counted in `errors`.
- A pure refusal raises `refused` and never `fused`.
- A budget refusal (`too-many-calls`) raises `fused`, `refused` and `unrepaired`, because no repair happened.
- The four verdict words are unchanged (`unmeasured`, `quiet`, `degraded`, `repaired`), evaluated in that order; only the counter line grew, to eight names plus the optional `resealed`.
- A bare member value is quoted only when exactly one segment reproduces the whole text as one plain object with a byte-identical payload.
- Zero candidates is refused as `bare-value-unproven`; two or more is refused as `ambiguous-bare-value` instead of guessed.
- A stream whose only defect was a reseal reads `repaired`, never `quiet`.
- The retry listener names a diagnosis exactly once per step and code, so a host-level retry of the same failure cannot fill the journal with the same sentence.
- A cancellation is never overridden by a retry.
- Control codes (`IMAGE_OFFLOAD_REQUIRED`, `INVALID_CREDENTIAL`, `MISSING_CREDENTIAL`) are passed through and never retried.
- `scan` reads a multi-frame zstd log through `decompressSessionLog`, the same reader the plugin ships.
- A directory scan keeps one auditable row per file.
- `--since` reports what it dropped as `before_since` instead of hiding it.
- An undecompressable file is a failure line and exit 3, never a silent zero.
- Redaction matches a home path escaped with one or two backslashes as well as the session directory that encodes it.
- The scan counts every `turn/end` (completed, `max_tokens`, aborted, error) and names every `reason.error.code`.
- The census is reported and never promoted into a finding, so the exit code still turns on `fused_calls` and `fusion_failures` alone.
- The byte budget is a gate, not a paragraph: it measures the modules a mounted plugin loads (residency), the modules only a command loads, and the total, and every emitted module must belong to exactly one of the first two.

## What it does not do

| Limit | Reality |
|---|---|
| Attribution | Stops at the assembled text: the plugin cannot prove whether the relay or the adapter glued the objects. |
| Truncation | A `max-tokens` cut is missing bytes and is not repaired. |
| Localized messages | The fallback parses the English `Received arguments:` text; a localized host message disables that fallback, though delta buffering still works. |
| Headless session files | A headless profile does not persist `assistant/attempt` streams, so the artifact reports 0 fused calls; the journal counters and the synthetic id carry the proof. |
| Synthetic IDs | `<id>#remedy-N` are traceability aids, not durable identities. |
| Desktop completion | The desktop artifact records `turn_end=aborted` because the operator stopped after the answer. |
| App cache | Verification applies to the recorded tarball's sha256, not to whatever a running app has cached. |
| Verdict granularity | One verdict word cannot express "observed and correctly refused"; only the counter line can. |
| Journal migration | Existing journal lines are not migrated; in a mixed journal `status --json` reports the shape of the last line. |
| Custom index tracking | An adapter that closes blocks itself and keeps its own index bookkeeping is still unmeasured (`BS-11`). |
| Request retries | Off by default. `SERVER`, `TRANSPORT` and `TIMEOUT` are already retried upstream, so this plugin only retries `MALFORMED_RESPONSE`, and only inside a budget you set. |
| Reasoning effort | The plugin can tell you a configured effort will be refused, but it never changes it for you. `agent/pre-step` is **not** mounted, and that is now a measured decision: P-0015 records what a rejection does — the turn closes as `blocked` with no step opened, the claimed input is discarded, and the CLI exits `1` — so a patch may use the seam, but it must rewrite the message with `{kind:'enter'}` rather than refuse. The desktop rendering of `blocked` is still unmeasured (`BS-17`). |
| Mid-stream withdrawal | Measured unreachable on this host: none of the persisted attempt streams carried a provable fusion inside a `block-end`, which is what `rolled-back` requires (`BS-14`). |

## Verify it yourself

```bash
dsh-remedy verify
dsh-remedy scan ~/.dsh/sessions --json
dsh-remedy explain --sessions ~/.dsh/sessions
pnpm run verify
node scripts/gate.mjs --mutate
```

Every artifact in `data/results/` is script-produced and has a `.sha256` sidecar. Two are worth opening first: the live run `data/results/live-2026-11-12T12-20-00.000Z.json` and the corpus replay `data/results/malformed-replay-2026-11-12T11-30-00.000Z.json`.

The whole `MALFORMED_RESPONSE` corpus on one machine was replayed through the built engine: 47 turns, 39 repaired, 8 refused, and no repaired case dispatched a call whose arguments failed to parse. A generated stress pass of 300000 argument texts asserts the same invariant with a recorded seed.

## Status

Four patches are `verified` on a real host: P-0001 on a headless profile and on the desktop app, P-0002 on a 2026-11-10 headless run that repaired a real two-call fusion and saw the synthesized call dispatched, P-0003 on a 2026-11-10 headless run whose journal wrote a non-zero `refused` after the code declined to repair a budget refusal, and P-0033 on an isolated harness whose endpoint replays the incomplete tool call of upstream discussion #13211: without the plugin the turn dies at V4 admission, with it the call carries a traceable id and the same session completes a second turn.

The other thirty-one are `tested`, not `verified`. Each carries unit tests, a negative control and a measured artifact where one exists: P-0004, P-0006 and P-0009 change an offline reader; P-0005 has no live bare-value shape yet; P-0007, P-0008, P-0012, P-0014, P-0017, P-0018, P-0019, P-0020, P-0024, P-0026, P-0028, P-0029, P-0031 and P-0035 are build-side or a corpus; P-0010, P-0016 and P-0025 change text a command prints; P-0011 and P-0013 sit on a seam a live journal witnesses only when a turn fails in a class this plugin retries, which the default budget of 0 never triggers; P-0015 is a measurement on an isolated profile rather than a mount; P-0027, P-0030 and P-0034 narrow what a repaired or failed turn is allowed to claim, with unit tests and a measured fixture but no live run of their own; and P-0032 moves prose, not behaviour.
Release status: `0.4.9` is published and is the registry `latest` for both `dsh-remedy` and `dsh-remedy-core`; it carries thirty-five patches and is measured on **DSH 0.2.2-rc.3**. A cold directory installed 0.4.9 from the registry and `dsh-remedy verify` printed `OK 6 fixture(s)`. The previous release is `0.4.8` with thirty-three patches, `0.4.7` with thirty-one, `0.4.6` with thirty, `0.4.5` with twenty-eight, `0.4.4` with twenty-seven, `0.4.3` with twenty-six, `0.4.2` with twenty-six, and `0.4.1` with twenty-three.

## Development

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm run verify
pnpm run gate
node scripts/gate.mjs --mutate
```

Six gates run on every change: `ssot`, `registry`, `namespace`, `step-review`, `copy`, `size`. `--mutate` breaks each one on purpose and requires every one to go red; it currently catches 6 of 6. The suite is 295 tests and 0 failing.

## Contributing

- Issues and pull requests are welcome.
- A behaviour change needs a failing test first.
- `pnpm run verify` must pass, and `node scripts/gate.mjs --mutate` must catch every gate.
- Gates use Node built-ins only; a new gate must be registered in `audit/gate_ledger.json`.
- No new runtime dependency in `dsh-remedy-core`.
- A patch cannot claim `verified` without a `data/results/live-*` artifact.
- Outward text is checked, not authored freely: every number in it must exist in `docs/copy/facts/public-repo-facts.md`, and the bytes must match `docs/copy/manifest.json`.

## Security

Security reports should use GitHub private vulnerability reporting on the public repository: https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/dsh-remedy/security/policy

evidence.readmeExcerpt: --- description: "The harness side of calling the AmberFlow browser engine: model-facing tools that observe a page, list and read flow apps, generate an app.mjs skeleton, validate a script's call sequence, run one flow app (with an execution budget), record a flow into a flow app, and run the real-site suite — for deployments that drive browser automation from a session." kind: "package-bundle" --- # @deepseek-ai/dsh-amberflow-bridge English | [中文](README.zh.md) ## Summary `dsh-amberflow-bridge` exposes an external browser engine as model-facing tools. AmberFlow has exactly ONE app format: a **flow script** at `$AMBERFLOW_HOME/apps//app.mjs` (or in the checkout's fixtures) exporting `meta` and `flow(ctx)`. The script owns the control flow — `if`, `for`, `while`, sub-functions — while the engine owns each step's target, gate, action and completion signal, and DOM signals are the only completion truth. The bridge adds no browser or app logic of its own and instead spawns that checkout's CLIs and summarizes their artifacts. The plugin ships **nine** tools: `amberflow_status` (environment/model facts), `amberflow_apps` (list flow apps through `amber apps list --json`), `amberflow_app_show` (metadata + current `app.mjs` source + version anchors), `amberflow_app_check` (load + dry-run the call sequence, no browser), `amberflow_inspect` (read-only page observation and hint candidates), `amberflow_session` (one state-preserving authoring session: open → observe → act → read/extract/signal → snapshot → close; never judges completion — that truth lives only in `amberflow_run`), `amberflow_app_create` (generate a flow skeleton with `amber apps new`), `amberflow_run` (run one app; `max_steps` is an execution budget), `amberflow_learn` (record a flow into a flow app, gated by a rules-only replay of the generated script), and `amberflow_test` (real-site regression suite). `amberflow_inspect` and `amberflow_session` `op:"observe"` share ONE element-row contract (`src/element-view.ts`: same field names — `hint_candidates`, not `hints` — same clipping, same 60/200 row cap, admission diagnostics passed through untouched; `ref` is a display anchor, act targets are hint strings). The plugin's **configuration page** (Settings → Plugins → this bundle's row → Configure) sets the three **online decision model** fields — Model URL, Token Key, ModelName (the same `AMBERFLOW_DECISION_*` keys `amber config set` writes for the engine CLI) — plus the execution parameters: the step gap and the HEADFUL switch. The authoring loop for an Agent is `amberflow_status` → `amberflow_apps` → `amberflow_app_show` (read `path` and the current source) → **edit `app.mjs` with the file tools** → `amberflow_app_check` → `amberflow_inspect` (look at the real page before writing a hint) → `amberflow_run` with `max_steps`/`trace` for structured feedback → `amberflow_run` full → `amberflow_test`. There is no step-number editing interface: a script has no static step table, steps are runtime facts, and the script version is the only flow version. ## Table of Contents - [Use this package](#use-this-package) - [Understand the implementation](#understand-the-implementation) - [Further Exploration](#further-exploration) - [Model Experience](#model-experience) - [Known Limitations and Deferred Work](#known-limitations-and-deferred-work) - [Dev Note](#dev-note) ----- ## Use this package Mount the plugin with the path of a AmberFlow checkout. A path that is not a checkout fails at load time rather than on the first call, so a typo surfaces during composition: ```yaml repoPath: null # optional; resolves config > AMBERFLOW_REPO > the checkout the plugin sits in nodeBin: null # optional; defaults to the running interpreter timeoutMs: 900000 # optional; live runs are slow by nature allowDangerous: false # optional; gates dry-run-gated tool steps toolPrefix: amberflow # optional; the model-visible tool-name prefix envMode: inherit # optional; `allowlist` strips session secrets from the child env forwardEnv: [] # optional; extra env var names forwarded in `allowlist` mode keepRuns: 30 # optional; newest $TMPDIR/dsh-amberflow-* dirs kept; 0 disables GC ``` ### When to choose it Choose it when a session should drive a flow that must stay reproducible: the engine refuses to invent a target, reports completion only from a DOM signal, and refuses to save a recorded flow unless a replay of the generated script with zero model calls still passes. Choose a pixel-level browser tool instead when the task depends on what a page looks like, or when no checkout is available to call. Install it into a profile as a bundle — `dsh plugin --profile add ` (the plugin window runs the same operation). Three channels are supported: - **Path / link** (this repository's development shape): `dsh plugin --profile web add /absolute/path/to/AmberFlow/integrations/dsh-bridge` installs the nested package; its `cordis.patch.yml` addresses the plugin by package name. - **The engine repository itself over git**: `dsh plugin --profile add github:Johnly1986/AmberFlow` installs the repo root, whose `dsh.bundle` points at `dsh-bundle.yml` — the row addresses `amberflow/dsh-plugin` (a package subpath), and the root package's `dsh.client` now serves the configuration page too. The clone contains the whole engine, so the plugin locates its own checkout; no build script runs, so no `allowBuilds` grant is needed for this package itself (its dependencies that do run install scripts — `onnxruntime-node`, `protobufjs` — are the only names to approve if pnpm lists them). Pin commits for installs you trust long-term (`#`), and run `npx playwright install chromium` once where the profile boots. The ONNX decision model is a large artifact that deliberately stays out of git: rules-only runs and `learn`'s zero-forward replay need nothing beyond the clone, but model-fallback decisions on a fresh machine want `laya_dec.onnx` (+ `.onnx.data`, optionally the tokenizer) installed — that is what the checkout's `npm run model:fetch -- --from ` does (SHA256-gated, verify-then-swap; `npm run doctor` names the missing piece). Without it the run still works and the summary says `model: off(missing)`; steps that genuinely need the model fail loudly at load instead of guessing. - **npm or tarball**: pack with `pnpm pack`; the root `package.json` is the bundle, so the git behavior above carries over unchanged. A package that declares `dsh.bundle` joins `dsh.profile.bundles` on install, so the tools become available without a hand-written profile patch; a live profile applies that at the next config reload. `AMBERFLOW_REPO` overrides the checkout the resolved config names; a path that is not a checkout fails at load time. ### Call it from another plugin Other plugins can inject the service instead of calling a tool. The bridge provides `ctx.amberflow` with `listApps`, `run`, `learn`, `status`, `appShow`, `appCheck`, `inspect`, `test`, and `createApp` — the same code the tools run, so the deployment gate and the failure diagnostics cannot drift between the two doors. The tools stay the model-facing door; the service is the plugin-facing one, and it needs no `callId`, no signal, and no tool name. ```ts import type { Context } from '@deepseek-ai/cordis' import '@deepseek-ai/dsh-amberflow-bridge' const Consumer = { name: 'consumer', inject: ['amberflow'], apply(ctx: Context) { return ctx.amberflow.run({ app: 'learned-cart', maxSteps: 3 }) }, } ``` ## Understand the implementation Each tool is a thin wrapper: it assembles an argv, runs one child process with a hard timeout, and summarizes the JSON the CLI wrote. Business semantics stay in the checkout; the bridge never scans the apps directory, never interprets app source, and never writes app code. - `amberflow_apps` spawns `amber apps list --json` and projects the envelope's rows: id, label, goal, writable path, source (`user` / `built-in`), `kind=flow`, invariant count, hosts, and an `error` for a script that failed to load. There is no static step count — steps are runtime facts — so a row never pretends to know how many steps will run. Listing starts no browser and calls no model. - `amberflow_app_show` spawns `amber apps show --json --code` and returns the path, metadata, `script_sha256` / `plan_sha256` (the "which version did I change" anchors) and the current script source. `path` is the only place to write; the Agent edits it with its own file tools. - `amberflow_app_check` spawns `amber apps check --json`: the script is loaded (import + `meta` contract + validation) and its `flow(ctx)` call sequence is dry-run, so problems come with the script line when the CLI can locate it. Exit code 2 means problems; the bridge reports them. - `amberflow_app_create` spawns `amber apps new --json` (optional `--goal` / `--host`) and then returns `app_show`. Only the flow skeleton is generated — there is no step/format/kind parameter, and no JSON app format. - `amberflow_run` spawns `src/app/app-runner.ts --app --out ` and reads `-result.json`. The summary lists failures only; the full per-step table stays in `-report.md`, which the result names so a caller can read it when the detail matters. `dry` dry-runs the script's call sequence (`--dry`, no browser) and returns it: that run writes no artifact and verifies nothing, so it is reported as an expansion rather than as a PASS or a FAIL. `max_steps` is an **execution budget** (`--max-steps`), not a step index; the trace flag defaults on for the bridge. - `amberflow_learn` spawns `tools/learn.ts --json --yes`, which performs the flow once, induces each step's completion signal and the end-state invariants, and writes a **flow app** (`app.mjs`) only when a rules-only replay of the generated script passes; the bridge reports that replay verbatim. `script` is required, because the CLI's only other action source is a human demonstration on an interactive terminal: a tool call has neither a terminal nor stdin, and the bridge always passes `--yes`. A call without a script is refused before anything is spawned. `apps_dir` overrides where the app lands (`--apps-dir`; the default is the user-scope `$AMBERFLOW_HOME/apps`). The bridge itself calls **no LLM**: the decision fallback is the checkout's local ONNX model, and `learn`'s save gate is a rules-only replay with zero model calls. LLM doors are CLI-level opt-ins that need `OPENAI_*` on the machine running the checkout — they are not a plugin requirement. ### Watching the browser (headed runs) Every browser door can be made visible with `--headful`: | Surface | How | |---|---| | Engine CLI | `amber run --headful`; `amber inspect --url --headed`; `node tools/learn.ts --headful` | | DSH tools | `…_run` with `headful: true`, `…_inspect` with `headful: true`, `…_learn` with `headful: true` (or `cdp` to drive a browser you already have open) | Two things to know: - **The window appears on the machine that runs the engine** — the deployment host — not inside the DSH browser page. Over a headless server, give it a display and look at that display: ```bash xvfb-run -a -s "-screen 0 1440x900x24" dsh --profile web --no-open --port 3080 # whole host under Xvfb # 或只包一次运行：xvfb-run -a amber test --tier smoke --headful # 要人眼看：再配 x11vnc / noVNC，或用 ffmpeg -f x11grab -i $DISPLAY 抓帧 ``` - Headed needs the **full chromium**. Measured here: `--headful` launches `chromium-*/chrome` with no `--headless` flag (a real window, captured on the virtual display), while the default launches `chrome-headless-shell --headless`. If a box only has the headless shell, a headed run stops with a message naming the fix (`npx playwright install chromium`) instead of a Playwright mystery. ### Configuration page: the unified decision service (System One) The bundle ships a browser half that registers its own row page at `plugins.row.config`, so Settings → Plugins → this bundle → the `amberflow-bridge` row gains a **Configure** control. The page shows exactly the `.volatile()` fields of the plugin's Config — the three **decision model** fields (the model the engine executes steps with) plus the execution parameters (the step gap and HEADFUL): | Field | Forwarded to the engine CLI as | Meaning | |---|---|---| | **Decision model URL** | `AMBERFLOW_DECISION_BASE_URL` | service base URL (e.g. `https://…/compatible-mode/v1` or `http://localhost:8008`); the bridge normalizes it to the `/systemone` endpoint (an already-suffixed value is kept as-is) | | **Decision Token Key** | `AMBERFLOW_DECISION_API_KEY` | bearer token; write-only — the Host never returns it, the UI shows only "configured / not set" | | **Decision ModelName** | `AMBERFLOW_DECISION_MODEL` | decision model id (e.g. `decision-model-preview`); empty uses the provider default | | **Step gap (ms)** | `AMBERFLOW_STEP_DELAY_MS` | minimum wait between two engine steps (0–60000); an app's own `meta.pace` still wins | | **HEADFUL (visible window)** | `AMBERFLOW_HEADFUL=1` | when ticked, every engine child process shows a browser window, overriding the engine config files' `runDefaults.headful=false` | HEADFUL is the **only** window switch: a browser window has one dimension ("visible or not"), so there is deliberately no headless counterpart boolean (two configs for one fact would overwrite each other). Unticked injects nothing: the engine decides from its own layering (CLI flags > env > config files) — for a permanently windowless host, set `AMBERFLOW_HEADFUL=0` in the engine rc instead. An explicit `headful` argument on a tool call is the CLI-flag layer and always wins over the injected env. How it behaves: - **Provider default:** with URL **and** token set, the bridge adds `--provider decision-service` to app runs (`amberflow_run`), so the plugin runs on the online decision model without a per-call argument. An explicit `provider` argument still wins, and ablation arms (`ablate`) never inherit the default. - **Effective without a restart.** `.volatile()` config fields are committed by the Loader into the running references and the bridge re-reads them on `loader/volatile-update`; CLI calls started afterwards see the new endpoint. Saves persist in the active profile's `cordis.patch.yml`. - **Unset = local plane.** Empty fields add no environment entries, so a deployment that configures nothing keeps the local ONNX decision model (or rules-only) — the bridge still needs no model key. - **Scope:** this is the **SystemOne execution** decision model. LLM doors are a separate path and still read `OPENAI_*` from the environment. - **Editing is loopback-only by Harness policy.** A page opened from a non-loopback address makes `ctx.remote.$host.isLoopback` false, and Harness switches settings to memory mode there: the Host configuration is neither read nor written over a remote page. The row page therefore renders a short explanation instead of the form when opened remotely — edit on the Host machine itself, or through an SSH tunnel (`ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:3080 `). What you save on a loopback page applies to every run, including runs started from the remote page. - **Only these `.volatile()` fields are editable here.** `repoPath`, `nodeBin`, `timeoutMs`, `allowDangerous`, `toolPrefix`, `envMode`, `envMode`-forwarding and `keepRuns` stay in `cordis.patch.yml` (changing an ordinary field remounts the plugin; `toolPrefix` even renames the tools, so it must not be live-edited). - **Both install doors serve this page.** The bundle ships two byte-equivalent client bundles: `client.js` for the nested `integrations/dsh-bridge` install (module id = package name, row key `@deepseek-ai/dsh-amberflow-bridge#amberflow-bridge`), and the generated `client-root.js` for the repository-root install (`dsh plugin add `; module id = root package `amberflow`, row key `amberflow#amberflow-bridge`). The repository bundle row names the PACKAGE ROOT (`amberflow`), because the DSH client scanner only serves a browser half for a package-root row — a hand-written profile patch that overrides this row must therefore use `name: amberflow` (the `amberflow/dsh-plugin` export alias keeps old Host-only patches loading, but they get no configuration page). Edit `client.js` only and regenerate with `node integrations/dsh-bridge/scripts/client-root-sync.mjs`; a test pins the generated copy. ### Trust boundary The bridge spawns a foreign process from `repoPath` and does not route it through the harness sandbox policy, so enabling the plugin means trusting that checkout. Dangerous tool steps stay refused unless the deployment sets `allowDangerous: true`, and a call that asks for them on a deployment that has not is rejected instead of being silently downgraded. ## Further Exploration - `docs/AGENT_INTERFACE.md` — the authoritative contract for this interface (apps, CLI JSON, bridge tools), and `docs/APP_SCRIPT_AUTHORING.md` — how a flow app's `meta` / `flow(ctx)` are written. - Inside the DSH installation this plugin runs in: `packages/core/tools` is the registry whose schemas and dispatch the bridge's tool definitions target. ## Model Experience The model sees a set of tools with narrow schemas: list/read (`apps` / `app_show`), validate (`app_check`), observe (`inspect`), author (`app_create` + its own file edits to `app.mjs`), run (`run` with an optional execution budget), record (`learn`), and regress (`test`). `amberflow_run` answers with PASS or FAIL, the completion count, invariant counts, the failed steps with their obstacle text, and the report path; steps that completed are a count, not rows, so a sixty-step flow costs a line rather than a page. Every answer also carries a **tier line** — `model: on` / `off(missing)` / `off(rules-only)` — and, when the artifact has it, the per-step **decision tally** (`rule 19 · model 1 (decision-service, conf 0.31) · reobserve 1 · cache 命中 6/12 forwards`): a user learns which ladder actually ran, and the model's appearances stop being invisible step-log trivia. A tool step that failed without being refused is named too, and a run that stopped with no failed step to name reports its exit code or timeout, so a FAIL says why it failed. `dry` answers with the script's dry-run call sequence instead, so a flow can be inspected without being run. `amberflow_learn` answers with the replay it was gated on, including the model-call count, so a flow that could not be reproduced is never reported as learned; without a script it refuses immediately, before a browser is launched. ## Known Limitations and Deferred Work - The live tests need a checkout and a chromium build (the recording test also needs the checkout's ONNX graph); without them they SKIP with the reason printed. - The bridge is deliberately not a `tool-*` package, so it stays out of the generated tool catalog. - Every run leaves its temp directory behind — the result names the report inside it, so that directory has to outlive the call. Artifacts are per call, never shared. `keepRuns` caps how many of the newest `dsh-amberflow-*` directories survive; a directory is only removed an hour after its last write, so a slow live run is never pruned under it. - The child environment is inherited wholesale by default (trusting the checkout is the stated premise). Set `envMode: allowlist` to forward only the run essentials plus `AMBERFLOW_*` and `forwardEnv`. - Upgrading the package while the Host is already running: the Host keeps the module generation it loaded at startup, so a newly added configuration page (and its Config schema) appears only after the Host process restarts. A fresh install has no such issue. - The bridge does not edit app source: there is no step/index editing tool, because a flow script has no static step table. The Agent reads and writes `app.mjs` itself. - `amberflow_learn` cannot demonstrate for you: recording a NEW flow needs a recorded action list, because the CLI's live recorder needs an interactive terminal. A script-less call is refused up front rather than being allowed to fail inside the engine. ### Dev Note 本包不再携带测试文件；在真实 DSH 进程里手工加载验证，或设 `DSH_ROOT` 后运行 `npm run setup && npm run build`。 # AmberFlow **浏览器自动化，每一步都能证明做对了。** AmberFlow 是一个**可验证的浏览器执行内核**：流程先被冻结，执行器按页面信号逐步完成任务；模型只参与元素选择与风险评估，不生成动作、也不替你做「完成」结论。每次运行都会留下可读、可追溯、可复现的证据。 它面向真实的工作流——登录后的受控系统、内部工具、测试环境——而不是「让 AI 随便点」的演示玩具。 --- ## 为什么需要 AmberFlow | 常见问题 | AmberFlow 的做法 | 你得到的结果 | |---|---|---| | AI Agent「看起来点完了」，但不知道是否真的成功 | 完成只认页面信号（URL / DOM），模型没有完成裁判权 | 绿就是绿，红就是红，可复核 | | RPA / 脚本改版即碎，失败也说不清原因 | 流程冻结 + 结构化停因 + 每次运行留痕 | 失败能定位、能复现、能交给别人看 | | 测试回归「跳过也算过」，证据散落在各处 | 退出码区分通过/失败/阻塞；每次运行三份证据 | CI 诚实门 + 可交付的证据包 | | 数据 / 凭据不能出域 | 私有部署、本地或自带模型；凭据本地按名读取 | 数据留在你自己的环境 | | 自动化一旦登录后就没人敢碰 | 登录/2FA/验证码可在用户授权下处理，凭据不进日志与报告 | 可以覆盖真实的登录后流程 | ## 适合谁 - **测试 / QA 团队与测试外包商**：把「录制一遍 → 登录后回归 → 产出证据」变成可交付物。 - **受监管 / 数据不出域的组织**：私有部署，证据可带走，凭据不经第三方。 - **Agent / 工具开发者**：把「可验证的浏览器执行」接入自己的 agent 工作流（DSH 桥已可用）。 **不适合**：无人值守的生产 RPA 平台、消费者个人自动化、任何需要绕过反爬或验证码黑产的场景。AmberFlow 的边界是明确的：**不绕反爬**、不伪造指纹、不轮换代理；验证环节只做用户授权内的「代过」。 ## 你会得到什么 - **一次录制，可重复回放**：演示一遍即可生成流程；规则档回放不通过就不会落盘。 - **每一步都有依据**：完成由页面信号判定，失败给出结构化原因和下一步建议。 - **三份证据**：`*-result.json`、`*-report.md`、`*-report.html`，敏感槽位自动掩码；需要时还可保留执行轨迹用于重放。 - **默认安全**：破坏性浏览器动作默认按干跑证据拒绝；需要显式放行才执行。凭据与敏感值默认不进产物。 - **可选私有部署**：本地模型或自带线上模型；Apache-2.0，可嵌进你自己的环境。 ## 5 分钟上手 需要 **Node ≥ 22.6** 与 Chromium。 ```bash git clone https://github.com/Johnly1986/AmberFlow.git cd AmberFlow npm ci npx playwright install chromium npm run doctor # 体检：Node / Chromium / 模型与配置 npm run examples-check # 离线跑通 4 个示例（零网络、零模型） ``` 从示例开始，把应用复制到你的用户目录： ```bash mkdir -p "$HOME/.amberflow/apps" cp -R examples/apps/01-basic-step "$HOME/.amberflow/apps/" # 在 checkout 里用这个入口（`npx amber` 在 checkout 内会挂住，原因见命令帮助） node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts apps check 01-basic-step node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts run 01-basic-step --dry-run node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts run 01-basic-step ``` > 仓库内为什么不用 `npx amber`：本包的 bin 没链进 `node_modules/.bin`，`npx` 会去解析远端同名包。就地用上面的 `node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts`，或者先 `npm link` 后直接用 `amber`。npm 包发布准备中（当前 2.0.0 未发布，建议从源码使用）。 创建自己的应用： ```bash node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts apps new my-app \ --goal "把商品加入购物车" --url https://shop.example.com/p/1 node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts inspect --url https://shop.example.com/p/1 --json # 编辑 $AMBERFLOW_HOME/apps/my-app/app.mjs 后： node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts apps check my-app node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts run my-app --trace ``` 应用就是用户目录下的 `app.mjs`（`meta` + `flow(ctx)`），不写进仓库、不依赖中央清单；仓库永远不内置应用。更多作者体验见 [examples/README.md](examples/README.md) 与 [docs/APP_SCRIPT_AUTHORING.md](docs/APP_SCRIPT_AUTHORING.md)。 ## 证据与安全 - **产物默认落盘**：每次运行写 `*-result.json` / `*-report.md` / `*-report.html`；证据默认不进仓库，失败截图/DOM 按敏感数据处理。 - **敏感值默认掩码**：槽位可在 `meta.secretSlots` 声明，产物/报告/stdout 中显示 `***`；CLI 敏感值建议用 `--slot-file`（JSON）而不是 `--slot`。 - **凭据模型**：凭据由用户在本机配置 / 环境变量 / 受支持存储保存，引擎按名读取；明文不进用例、计划、报告、trace 或仓库。详见 [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md)。 - **反爬与验证边界**：不绕反爬、不伪造指纹、不轮换代理、不规避风控/限流；验证环节（登录/2FA/验证码）可在用户授权下由人工步或注入处理器代过。站点 ToS 由使用者负责。 - **默认安全**：破坏性浏览器动作默认拒绝；确需放行时显式使用 `--confirm-unsafe`（或 `AMBERFLOW_CONFIRM_SAFE=0`），并自行承担风险。 ## 当前状态 AmberFlow 2.0.0 是**未发布**版本，正在从「可运行」走向「可交付」： - 已具备：可验证执行内核、录制→回放、证据报告、真实站点回归套件、DSH Agent 桥、离线示例与离线校验、默认安全与凭据脱敏。 - 规划/待补：认证后的回归闭环（会话复用、验证处理器、认证感知录制）、HTML 证据报告增强、npm 正式发布、私有部署交付包。 - **明确不做**：无人值守 RPA 平台、消费者个人自动化、任何绕过反爬的灰色需求。当前不承诺 SLA/驻场，只适合受控环境的小团队试点。 完整变更见 [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md)。 ## 文档 - [离线示例与用法](examples/README.md) - [应用脚本作者指南](docs/APP_SCRIPT_AUTHORING.md) - [Agent / DSH 接入契约](docs/AGENT_INTERFACE.md) - [人工步骤与运行节奏](docs/MANUAL_STEPS_AND_PACE.md) - [决策服务配置](docs/DECISION_SERVICE_CONFIG.md) - [梯队A（v2）落地实施文档](docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN-TIER-A-v2.md) - [安全策略](SECURITY.md) - [变更记录](CHANGELOG.md) ## 开发与贡献 ```bash npm run check # PR 门禁：类型检查 + 配置一致性 + 提示词/信号校验 + 泄露扫描 + 示例校验 + 用例声明 npm run test -- --tier smoke # 真实站点（需要网络；跳过 ≠ 通过） ``` 仓库没有单元测试与离线夹具是**设计决定**：真实站点套件是唯一测试层；运行证据不进仓库。发现问题请通过 issue 反馈，安全问题请走 [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) 的报告渠道。 ## License Apache-2.0，见 [LICENSE](LICENSE)。

# AmberFlow

**浏览器自动化，每一步都能证明做对了。**

AmberFlow 是一个**可验证的浏览器执行内核**：流程先被冻结，执行器按页面信号逐步完成任务；模型只参与元素选择与风险评估，不生成动作、也不替你做「完成」结论。每次运行都会留下可读、可追溯、可复现的证据。

它面向真实的工作流——登录后的受控系统、内部工具、测试环境——而不是「让 AI 随便点」的演示玩具。

---

## 为什么需要 AmberFlow

| 常见问题 | AmberFlow 的做法 | 你得到的结果 |
|---|---|---|
| AI Agent「看起来点完了」，但不知道是否真的成功 | 完成只认页面信号（URL / DOM），模型没有完成裁判权 | 绿就是绿，红就是红，可复核 |
| RPA / 脚本改版即碎，失败也说不清原因 | 流程冻结 + 结构化停因 + 每次运行留痕 | 失败能定位、能复现、能交给别人看 |
| 测试回归「跳过也算过」，证据散落在各处 | 退出码区分通过/失败/阻塞；每次运行三份证据 | CI 诚实门 + 可交付的证据包 |
| 数据 / 凭据不能出域 | 私有部署、本地或自带模型；凭据本地按名读取 | 数据留在你自己的环境 |
| 自动化一旦登录后就没人敢碰 | 登录/2FA/验证码可在用户授权下处理，凭据不进日志与报告 | 可以覆盖真实的登录后流程 |

## 适合谁

- **测试 / QA 团队与测试外包商**：把「录制一遍 → 登录后回归 → 产出证据」变成可交付物。
- **受监管 / 数据不出域的组织**：私有部署，证据可带走，凭据不经第三方。
- **Agent / 工具开发者**：把「可验证的浏览器执行」接入自己的 agent 工作流（DSH 桥已可用）。

**不适合**：无人值守的生产 RPA 平台、消费者个人自动化、任何需要绕过反爬或验证码黑产的场景。AmberFlow 的边界是明确的：**不绕反爬**、不伪造指纹、不轮换代理；验证环节只做用户授权内的「代过」。

## 你会得到什么

- **一次录制，可重复回放**：演示一遍即可生成流程；规则档回放不通过就不会落盘。
- **每一步都有依据**：完成由页面信号判定，失败给出结构化原因和下一步建议。
- **三份证据**：`*-result.json`、`*-report.md`、`*-report.html`，敏感槽位自动掩码；需要时还可保留执行轨迹用于重放。
- **默认安全**：破坏性浏览器动作默认按干跑证据拒绝；需要显式放行才执行。凭据与敏感值默认不进产物。
- **可选私有部署**：本地模型或自带线上模型；Apache-2.0，可嵌进你自己的环境。

## 5 分钟上手

需要 **Node ≥ 22.6** 与 Chromium。

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Johnly1986/AmberFlow.git
cd AmberFlow
npm ci
npx playwright install chromium
npm run doctor          # 体检：Node / Chromium / 模型与配置
npm run examples-check  # 离线跑通 4 个示例（零网络、零模型）
```

从示例开始，把应用复制到你的用户目录：

```bash
mkdir -p "$HOME/.amberflow/apps"
cp -R examples/apps/01-basic-step "$HOME/.amberflow/apps/"

# 在 checkout 里用这个入口（`npx amber` 在 checkout 内会挂住，原因见命令帮助）
node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts apps check 01-basic-step
node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts run 01-basic-step --dry-run
node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts run 01-basic-step
```

> 仓库内为什么不用 `npx amber`：本包的 bin 没链进 `node_modules/.bin`，`npx` 会去解析远端同名包。就地用上面的 `node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts`，或者先 `npm link` 后直接用 `amber`。npm 包发布准备中（当前 2.0.0 未发布，建议从源码使用）。

创建自己的应用：

```bash
node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts apps new my-app \
  --goal "把商品加入购物车" --url https://shop.example.com/p/1
node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts inspect --url https://shop.example.com/p/1 --json
# 编辑 $AMBERFLOW_HOME/apps/my-app/app.mjs 后：
node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts apps check my-app
node --experimental-strip-types src/cli/main.ts run my-app --trace
```

应用就是用户目录下的 `app.mjs`（`meta` + `flow(ctx)`），不写进仓库、不依赖中央清单；仓库永远不内置应用。更多作者体验见 [examples/README.md](examples/README.md) 与 [docs/APP_SCRIPT_AUTHORING.md](docs/APP_SCRIPT_AUTHORING.md)。

## 证据与安全

- **产物默认落盘**：每次运行写 `*-result.json` / `*-report.md` / `*-report.html`；证据默认不进仓库，失败截图/DOM 按敏感数据处理。
- **敏感值默认掩码**：槽位可在 `meta.secretSlots` 声明，产物/报告/stdout 中显示 `***`；CLI 敏感值建议用 `--slot-file`（JSON）而不是 `--slot`。
- **凭据模型**：凭据由用户在本机配置 / 环境变量 / 受支持存储保存，引擎按名读取；明文不进用例、计划、报告、trace 或仓库。详见 [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md)。
- **反爬与验证边界**：不绕反爬、不伪造指纹、不轮换代理、不规避风控/限流；验证环节（登录/2FA/验证码）可在用户授权下由人工步或注入处理器代过。站点 ToS 由使用者负责。
- **默认安全**：破坏性浏览器动作默认拒绝；确需放行时显式使用 `--confirm-unsafe`（或 `AMBERFLOW_CONFIRM_SAFE=0`），并自行承担风险。

## 当前状态

AmberFlow 2.0.0 是**未发布**版本，正在从「可运行」走向「可交付」：

- 已具备：可验证执行内核、录制→回放、证据报告、真实站点回归套件、DSH Agent 桥、离线示例与离线校验、默认安全与凭据脱敏。
- 规划/待补：认证后的回归闭环（会话复用、验证处理器、认证感知录制）、HTML 证据报告增强、npm 正式发布、私有部署交付包。
- **明确不做**：无人值守 RPA 平台、消费者个人自动化、任何绕过反爬的灰色需求。当前不承诺 SLA/驻场，只适合受控环境的小团队试点。

完整变更见 [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md)。

## 文档

- [离线示例与用法](examples/README.md)
- [应用脚本作者指南](docs/APP_SCRIPT_AUTHORING.md)
- [Agent / DSH 接入契约](docs/AGENT_INTERFACE.md)
- [人工步骤与运行节奏](docs/MANUAL_STEPS_AND_PACE.md)
- [决策服务配置](docs/DECISION_SERVICE_CONFIG.md)
- [梯队A（v2）落地实施文档](docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN-TIER-A-v2.md)
- [安全策略](SECURITY.md)
- [变更记录](CHANGELOG.md)

## 开发与贡献

```bash
npm run check              # PR 门禁：类型检查 + 配置一致性 + 提示词/信号校验 + 泄露扫描 + 示例校验 + 用例声明
npm run test -- --tier smoke   # 真实站点（需要网络；跳过 ≠ 通过）
```

仓库没有单元测试与离线夹具是**设计决定**：真实站点套件是唯一测试层；运行证据不进仓库。发现问题请通过 issue 反馈，安全问题请走 [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) 的报告渠道。

## License

Apache-2.0，见 [LICENSE](LICENSE)。
